stances.claim: Panic is not warranted by Duterte's eventual naming of 13 of 15 SC justices, but public vigilance is.
stances.rhetorical_move: calibrated response -- fear-reduction paired with civic responsibility

stances.claim: Presidential attempts to dominate the judiciary are not new -- every president, here and in the US, names justices expected to support their programs.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical normalization to contextualize the present concern

stances.claim: Even Marcos could not prevent the rise of judicial heroes among his own appointees -- Concepcion, Teehankee, Muñoz-Palma, and Melencio-Herrera.
Even GMA, who named a majority and eventually all 15 justices, could not get everything she wanted -- she lost on the people's initiative for parliamentary shift and on emergency powers.

The ultimate test of judicial independence is the Court's brinkmanship in balancing protection of people's rights against axiomatic respect for executive actions -- guided by the four constitutional standards.
Public vigilance insisting on the four constitutional standards (proven competence, integrity, probity, independence) will protect people's rights and secure justices' place in history.

notable_anecdotes: Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) -- the Court validated the 1973 Constitution ratified by a raising of hands in barangay assemblies rather than secret ballots in a nationwide plebiscite, the paradigm case of judicial capitulation under Marcos.

Despite Marcos's dominance, judicial heroes emerged: CJ Roberto Concepcion, Justices Claudio Teehankee, Cecilia Muñoz-Palma, and Ameurfina Melencio-Herrera -- proof that appointment does not guarantee loyalty.

GMA naming a majority and eventually all 15 justices in 9.5 years (second in tenure only to Marcos's 21), yet the Court still blocked her people's initiative for parliamentary shift and struck down her emergency powers issuance.
Three of the JBC's seven members already Duterte allies; the IBP slot held by Fernan-Cayosa appeared to be the only member outside the President's loop.

decision_framework_signals: Calibrate public response to executive judicial dominance: vigilance, not panic
Use historical precedent (Marcos, GMA) to show presidential appointment power has never guaranteed full court control

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to alarmed reader reactions to his August 5 column forecasting that President Duterte would name a majority of SC justices before his midterm -- and eventually 13 of 15 by end of term -- Panganiban urges vigilance but not panic. He acknowledges the 'foreboding cases' cited by readers (Marcos burial, Mindanao martial law, Sereno ouster) and notes the JBC's political tilt (three Duterte allies among seven, with only the IBP slot held by Fernan-Cayosa appearing outside the President's loop). But he places this in historical context: presidential attempts to dominate the judiciary are not new anywhere in the world, and the Philippines has experienced this before. Under Marcos, Javellana v. Executive Secretary (March 31, 1973) validated a constitution ratified by hand-raising rather than secret ballots -- yet judicial heroes still emerged among Marcos's own appointees: CJ Roberto Concepcion, Justices Teehankee, Muñoz-Palma, and Melencio-Herrera. Under GMA, who had the second-longest incumbency and named a majority and eventually all 15 justices (including three chiefs), the Court still blocked her people's initiative for parliamentary shift and struck down her emergency powers issuance. The ascendancy of the Court ultimately depends on the justices' adherence to the four constitutional standards of 'proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence.' The Court's brinkmanship -- balancing protection of people's rights against the prima facie presumption of regularity of executive actions -- is the ultimate test of independence. Public vigilance insisting on those four standards will protect rights and secure justices' places in history; while not all will be judicial heroes, no one wants to be remembered as a judicial villain.
